englishChanges.before: I wasn't the first to break down. Crito had already gotten up, unable to hold back his tears. 'What is this strange outcry?' he said. 'I sent the women away precisely to prevent this kind of thing. I've been told that a man should die in peace. Be quiet, and have patience.' We were ashamed when we heard him, and held back our tears. He walked about until, as he said, his legs grew heavy, and then he lay on his back, as instructed. The man who had given him the poison checked his feet and legs from time to time. After a while he pressed his foot hard and asked if he could feel it. 'No,' Socrates said. Then the man pressed his legs, and so upward, showing us that he was growing cold and stiff. Socrates felt it himself and said: 'When the cold reaches my heart, that will be the end.' He was growing cold around the midsection when he uncovered his face — he had drawn the cloth over himself — and spoke his last words: 'Crito, I owe a rooster to Asclepius. Will you remember to pay the debt?' 'It shall be paid,' said Crito. 'Is there anything else?' There was no answer. After a moment or two, there was a slight movement. The attendants uncovered him. His eyes were fixed. Crito closed his eyes and mouth.
englishChanges.after: I wasn't the first. Crito had stood up when he could no longer hold back his tears, and I followed him. Then Apollodorus, who had been weeping all along, let out a loud, anguished cry that made us all lose our courage. Only Socrates stayed calm. 'What is this strange outcry?' he said. 'I sent the women away chiefly so they wouldn't behave like this. I've been told that a person should die in peace. Be quiet, then, and endure.' We were ashamed when we heard him and held back our tears. He walked until he said his legs were beginning to fail, then lay on his back as instructed. The man who had given him the poison examined his feet and legs from time to time. After a while he pressed his foot hard and asked whether he could feel it. 'No,' Socrates said. Then he pressed his leg and worked upward, showing us that Socrates was cold and stiff. The man touched him again and said that when the poison reached his heart, he would be gone. The cold had almost reached his groin when Socrates uncovered his face, which he had covered with a cloth, and spoke his last words: 'Crito, we owe a rooster to Asclepius. Pay the debt, and don't neglect it.' 'It will be done,' said Crito. 'Is there anything else you want to say?' There was no reply. A little later he moved, and the attendant uncovered him. His eyes were fixed. Seeing this, Crito closed his mouth and eyes.
